title: Converting a one-car garage into a small machine shop: power, layout, budget
summary: A phased schedule for turning a one-car garage into a usable small shop — power and layout follow the calendar, not a floorplan sketch.

blocks.eyebrow: Schedule first, then wire and place
blocks.title: Build the shop in phases you can finish
blocks.body: A one-car garage becomes a small machine shop when power, floor load, and machine placement arrive in the right order. This page starts with the calendar. Floorplan sketches wait until the phases that need them.

items.label: Example subpanel target for a light metal shop

items.title: Decide what the shop is for
items.detail: Lathe and mill? Weld cell? Wood only? The answer sets voltage, dust, and floor loads before you buy a single breaker.

items.title: Phase 1 — Make it safe to work in
items.detail: Clear junk, fix leaks, add lighting you can actually see by, and confirm the door and egress still work with machines inside.

items.title: Phase 2 — Power that matches the tools
items.detail: Load calc, subpanel or feeder decision, and receptacles placed for the machines you already own or have on order.

items.title: Phase 3 — Layout that leaves aisle space
items.detail: Place heavy machines first, then benches and storage. Leave a path wide enough to walk past a running spindle without sideways dancing.

items.title: Phase 4 — Prove the shop with real work
items.detail: One simple job end-to-end: stock in, chips out, part measured. Fix what the first job reveals before buying the next tool.

blocks.heading: Phase 1 detail: safe shell
blocks.body: Before any machine rolls in, the garage has to be a dry, lit room with a floor that will not surprise you. Patch roof leaks, seal the biggest air leaks around the door, and replace a single bare bulb with at least two LED shop lights on separate switches. Confirm the slab can take point loads — a benchtop mill on casters is different from a 1,200 lb lathe on three pads.

nodes.title: List nameplate amps
nodes.detail: Every tool you own or will buy in year one — voltage and FLA from the plate, not from memory.

nodes.title: Load calculation
nodes.detail: Sum continuous loads with diversity. Example light shop often lands near a 60 A 240 V feeder; verify locally.

nodes.title: Subpanel vs. shared
nodes.detail: A dedicated subpanel in the garage keeps shop breakers out of the house panel and makes lockout saner.

nodes.title: Receptacle map
nodes.detail: Place 120 V and 240 V outlets for the Phase 3 machine positions — do not wire the walls until machines have footprints.

blocks.caption: Dollar ranges are examples for a hobby-scale garage shop in 2026 dollars, not a quote. Local electrical work and permits dominate the real number.

blocks.heading: Phase 3 detail: layout after power
blocks.body: With receptacles rough-located, roll in the heaviest machine first and chalk the swing of its handles and chip throw. Put the lathe or mill where the 240 V lands without an extension cord. Benches and storage fill the leftover wall runs. Aisle width matters more than symmetry — if you cannot walk past a running machine carrying a long bar, the layout failed.

blocks.heading: Layout checks before you bolt anything down

items.label: Chip and coolant path does not cross the walking aisle
items.detail: Or you will track metal into the house forever.

items.label: Door still opens fully with machines placed
items.detail: Egress and delivery both care about this.

items.label: No extension cords for 240 V tools
items.detail: If the cord is required, the receptacle is in the wrong place — move the outlet or the machine.

items.label: One clear wall for future growth
items.detail: Shops that fill every inch in month one become storage units by month six.

blocks.heading: Phase 4: first real job
items: Pick a simple part you already understand — a bushing, a bracket, a fixture plate.
Run stock to finished dimension and measure it with the tools you actually own.
Write down what failed: lighting glare, missing outlet, wobbly bench, no place for chips.
Fix those before the next tool purchase. The shop earns upgrades by surviving work.

columns.name: Power and safety
columns.detail: Often the largest early check: feeder, panel, receptacles, lighting, and any required permits or electrician time.

columns.name: Machines
columns.detail: Can dwarf everything else if you buy new. Used iron with known backlash often beats a shiny import that fights you.

columns.name: Consumables and time
columns.detail: Tooling, cutting fluid, PPE, and weekends. A shop that only exists on paper still costs evenings.

blocks.title: Electrical work is local
blocks.body: Load calculations, grounding, and permit rules vary by jurisdiction. Treat the amps and dollar figures here as planning examples. If you are not qualified to pull a feeder, hire someone who is — a shop fire is not a learning project.

blocks.title: Why this page is not a floorplan first
blocks.body: Pretty layouts drawn before the power plan tend to put a mill where no 240 V will ever land. The schedule forces decisions in the order that keeps you from rewiring twice.

blocks.heading: Buy order that respects the schedule
rows: Tooling kits for machines you do not own yet
A second large machine that steals aisle space
Specialty tooling for the work you actually do
blocks.caption: Money follows completed phases. Buying the lathe before the feeder is how shops stall.

blocks.heading: Common ways this project stalls
items: Drawing a pretty floorplan, then discovering the only 240 V outlet is on the wrong wall.
Parking a car in the bay again after Phase 1, which quietly turns the shop back into storage.
Skipping the first measured part and calling the room finished because the tools look good in photos.

blocks.heading: Phase check
blocks.prompt: You have lighting and a cleared floor, but no load calculation yet. A friend offers you a free 240 V lathe this weekend. What do you do?
options: Roll it in immediately — free iron never waits
Finish Phase 2 power planning first, then accept delivery when a receptacle exists
Store it in the driveway indefinitely and call the shop done
Wire an extension cord from the dryer outlet and hope
blocks.explanation: Phase 2 exists so heavy tools arrive to power that matches them. A free lathe on an extension cord is how weekend shops earn expensive lessons.
blocks.correctFeedback: Right — the schedule protects you from free-iron urgency.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Re-read Phase 2. Power before placement keeps you from rewiring under a machine.

blocks.heading: Done looks like chips on the floor
blocks.body: When Phase 4 produces one measured part without extension cords or darkness, the garage is a shop. Everything after that is iteration.
